https://www.thenorthernecho.co.uk/news/2.text: Scouts Clubs and societies Leisure Whitley Bay Stu Bennet to represent UK at World Scout Jamboree in 2027 By Gavin Engelbrecht Reporter Share 0 Comments Whitley Bay Scout leader Stu Bennet has been selected to represent the UK at the 2027 World Scout Jamboree in Poland, joining 600 volunteers helping to deliver the global event for more than 50,000 Scouts from around the world. (Image: Supplied) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A North East Scout leader has been selected to help deliver one of the world's largest youth events after being chosen to represent the UK at the 2027 World Scout Jamboree in Poland. Stu Bennet from Whitley Bay will join a team of 600 UK volunteers supporting the jamboree, which will bring together more than 50,000 Scouts from around the globe for an immersive global adventure in Gdansk, Poland. The event is aimed at young people aged 14 to 17. Mr Bennet said: "I’ve been fortunate enough to be involved in international Scouting a few times over the years. "This is my second World Scout Jamboree and I’m really looking forward to providing more opportunities for young people to develop skills, make friends and lifelong memories – but also be able to do that myself. "Scouting has opened so many doors for me, and I hope that I can be a small part of making this adventure memorable for all the young people taking part." The World Scout Jamboree is held every four years in a different country and offers young people the opportunity to explore new cultures, develop life skills, and build friendships across borders. Chief Scout Dwayne Fields congratulated all the UK volunteers selected for the event. Mr Fields said: "Congratulations to Stu and all the UK volunteers heading to the World Scout Jamboree in Poland. "Opportunities like this are what Scouting is all about, bringing people together, building confidence, and showing young people what’s possible when they step outside their comfort zone. "The Jamboree is more than an event, it's a chance to connect with the world, to learn from different cultures, and to come back inspired to make a difference at home. Read more Summer theatre workshops in North Yorkshire bring spells and fairy tales North East beach named one of the best for summer holidays in national ranking Teesside festival set for spectacular return with aerial shows, circus and family fun "I’ve no doubt Stu will grab this experience with both hands and make the most of every moment." As part of the international team, Mr Bennet will help run activities, support cultural exchanges, and deliver large-scale events for young people. Organisers have described the jamboree as a "once-in-a-lifetime opportunity" for Scouts to experience global citizenship, outdoor adventure, and the power of international friendship. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/09/08/oros.text: Menü Kereső Rácz András szerint diplomáciai fedésben dolgozó hírszerzők a kiutasított orosz diplomaták Belföld Külföld frissítve Kovács Pál Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Orbán Anita külügyminiszter nyilatkozatából a diplomáciai nyelvezet szabályai szerint az következik, hogy a kedden Magyarországról kiutasított tíz orosz diplomata valójában diplomáciai fedésben dolgozott, és hírszerzői tevékenységet folytatott – mondta a keddi kiutasításokra reagálva Rácz András, a Magyar Külügyi Intézet vezérigazgató-helyettese az MTI-nek. Az ügy hátteréről itt olvashatnak részletesen . Orbán Anita külügyminiszter kedden jelentette be , hogy utasítására a Külügyminisztérium illetékes vezetője tájékoztatta Oroszország budapesti nagykövetét, hogy a magyar hatóságok értékelése szerint az orosz képviselet 10 munkatársa olyan tevékenységet folytatott Magyarországon, amely a Bécsi Egyezmény alapján diplomatától nem elfogadható. Rácz András szerint a „diplomáciai státusszal nem összeegyeztethető tevékenység” megfogalmazás hagyományosan a hírszerzői tevékenységet jelenti. Úgy véli, Magyarország ezzel a lépéssel gyakorlatilag csatlakozik az európai uniós szövetségesekhez abban a tevékenységben, hogy csökkentse az Oroszországi Föderáció hírszerző kapacitásait az Európai Unió és a NATO tagországainak területén – mondta. A Külügyi Intézet vezérigazgató-helyettese úgy véli, pályafutása alatt nem történt ilyen nagy léptékű kiutasítás az országban. Az Orbán-kormány alatt történt néhány úgynevezett csendes kiutasítás, azonban erről pontos információk nem állnak rendelkezésre – mondta. A mostani kiutasítás szerinte barátságtalan lépés, de négy és fél évvel ezelőtt kellett volna megtörténnie. Így most Magyarország régi adósságát törleszti az EU- és NATO-szövetségesek felé, mondta Rácz, mivel a Budapesten diplomáciai fedésben működő orosz hírszerzők rendszeresen hajtanak végre műveleteket máshol a schengeni övezetben és a schengeni övezeten kívüli balkáni országokban is. Marija Zaharova, az orosz külügyminisztérium szóvivője a kiutasítás hírére reagálva kemény és fájdalmas válaszlépést ígért . Az ehhez hasonló diplomáciai kiutasításokra az ellenválasz általában hasonló mértékű diplomáciai lépés, tehát az oroszok várhatóan hasonló létszámban utasíthatnak majd ki magyar diplomatákat, vagy olyanokat, akiket hírszerzőnek tartanak. Orbán Anita szerint a diplomaták kiutasítása nem jelenti az Oroszországgal fennálló diplomáciai kapcsolatok megszakítását. Magyarország továbbra is fenn kívánja tartani a szükséges párbeszédet a kölcsönös tisztelet és a szabályok betartása mellett. Magyar Péter a parlamentben is felolvasta Orbán Anita bejegyzését, azt mondta, hogy a Tisza-kormány megvédi az ország szuverenitását. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Nigel Farage said he had been warning about ‘Iranian agents’ coming into the UK on small boats after arrests near RAF Fairford. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Nigel Farage said he had been warning about ‘Iranian agents’ coming into the UK on small boats after arrests near RAF Fairford. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian Politics Nandy labels Farage ‘master of conspiracy theory’ over Fairford claims Culture secretary criticises Reform leader after he tried to link suspected bomb plot to small boat crossings Ben Quinn and Alexandra Topping Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.16 EDT Last modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nigel Farage has been described as a “master of the conspiracy theory” by the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, after he tried to link events at RAF Fairford to small boat crossings. The Reform UK leader was criticised over his reaction to the arrests of the men on Sunday, when he said he had been warning for months about “Iranian agents” coming into the UK across the Channel in small boats. “We deserve to be told the truth about the Fairford bomb plotters’ identities,” he added in his post on X on Sunday. On Monday he posted a video in which he claimed to have received intelligence that the Iranian regime was using the small boats “to get their operatives into Britain”. Less than an hour later, Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) said that the five suspects were all British nationals. The men – three residents of Westminster and two others from Camden and Willesden, all London boroughs – have since been released on bail while the police investigate “multiple lines of inquiry”. Nandy told the Guardian at Labour party conference on Monday that Farage was a “master of the conspiracy theory” when asked about his comments. “I think that he’s good at using the very real sentiment that a lot of people feel, of anxiety and distrust,” she added. “Particularly in this era of mis- and disinformation, I think he’s very agile at exploiting that for political gain.” Defending the authorities’ not having immediately released identity details of the suspects, Nandy said the first job of the government was to reassure the public that they were taking the right steps to keep them safe, which sometimes means “withholding information where it is in the public interest”. “More information is usually better than not,” she added, but it was “not always a conspiracy” when it was held back. Police involved in the investigation have also appealed for patience, without the pressure from speculation, while they conduct their inquiries. CTP senior national coordinator, deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans, said in an update: “I am very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised. However, I ask that at this time, Counter Terrorism Policing are given the space to work carefully and clearly.” Farage was also accused of “irresponsible nonsense” by Jenny Jones, a Green Party peer, who said: “Once again Farage’s attempts to whip up division by scapegoating some of the world’s most vulnerable people has left him with egg on his face.” Speaking after the police said that the suspects were British nationals, Farage denied any suggestion it had been irresponsible speculate about the incident while the government was carefully calibrating its responses to the security operation in Gloucestershire. “I have been saying it for years. I didn’t say anything different yesterday. What I have been saying for years and saying all summer, our national security is threatened from the outside by weakness on borders like it has never been before,” he told Sky News. Other Reform UK MPs including Robert Jenrick and Richard Tice also rushed to try to link the RAF Fairford incident to small boat crossings. Jenrick said that “we may now be seeing the consequences” of “complacency” by the Home Office after he had previously said terrorist were using small boats to enter the UK. Later on Monday, Tice shared an X post by his partner Isabel Oakeshott, who said UK law recognised six types of British nationality and that asking for the suspects’ “countries of origin” was among “perfectly reasonable questions”. The Reform deputy leader added: “Ethnicity? Dual nationals? Asylum seekers? Previous convictions? Known to Prevent / Authorities? Benefits claimants? Living in social housing?” Explore more on these topics Politics Nigel Farage Reform UK Lisa Nandy Labour Labour conference 2026 news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK US politics World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine Football Newsletters Business Environment UK politics Science Tech Global development Obituaries

https://www.politico.eu/article/4-reason.text: LONDON — Andy Burnham pledged to bring back hope when he entered Downing Street. Labour MPs are feeling it — for now. The British prime minister is approaching 100 days in No. 10 this week with his party believing things are on the up. Keir Starmer was toppled earlier this year after disastrous local election results precipitated a loss of confidence in his administration. Advertisement Advertisement Disgruntled Labour MPs warned their new leader must show up, listen to them and accept some disagreement to avoid repeating his predecessor’s mistakes. POLITICO sets out the four reasons Labour MPs are feeling more chipper under Burnham — but they still see potential pitfalls ahead. Some of the dozen parliamentarians interviewed by POLITICO for this piece were granted anonymity to speak candidly about the internal party matters. 1) Disagreement is tolerated MPs reckon Burnham’s administration is more willing to recognize different views within the broad church Labour Party. Burnham himself told a Parliamentary Labour Party meeting that disagreement is fine as long as MPs speak to him about it, according to Simon Opher — a 2024-intake MP and member of Mainstream, the soft-left faction supported by Burnham when he was Greater Manchester mayor. “It sounds weird, but that is a remarkable difference from what they had before,” Opher said, claiming he felt a “slight climate of fear” early in his political career. Advertisement Advertisement Starmer infuriated MPs when weeks after taking office he suspended the whip from those who voted to scrap a two-child benefit cap — only to U-turn earlier this year. By contrast, Kim Johnson, a member of Labour’s left-wing Socialist Campaign Group faction, points out she wasn’t sanctioned after abstaining on the government’s Courts and Tribunals Bill earlier this month because she believes it still weakens the right to trial by jury. “You’re not feeling you can’t do that or risk losing the whip,” she said. Burnham’s eyes are photographed as he delivers a speech at the Labour Conference in Liverpool on Sept. 29, 2026. | Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images Of course, Burnham’s appetite for disagreement hasn’t been fully put to the test. He entered No. 10 at the start of the summer recess, when MPs were away from Westminster, and there was a month-long conference recess when they returned to SW1 in September. And MPs don’t want a totally laissez-faire regime. Advertisement Advertisement “I didn’t get into politics to sit in a room and just agree with each other,” said another 2024-intake Labour MP. “I don’t think you get good policy by just sitting around like nodding dogs.” But they said they “genuinely believe in collective responsibility,” and are “quite relaxed” about the consequences of voting against the whip. Another backbench MP warns Burnham’s lax approach can only last so long. “Andy is riding high still, he is not in [Nigel] Farage or [Zack] Polanski territory, he can afford for people to go ‘I don’t like this.’ It’s when the shit hits the fan, and the public are saying they’re not happy, then you begin to find the political patience wears out,” that backbencher added. Burnham may yet regret his promise that the whips office will act as an HR department, the MP said, “because you want them to come down like a clonking fist.” 2) Ministers are more visible Burnham’s team is making itself seen, his MPs report. Whips have been calling them to check in, and Burnham himself has attended PLP sub-group meetings. Cabinet ministers have also been available for meetings. Advertisement Advertisement Though another Socialist Campaign Group MP admitted “it’s a very low bar” for improvement. “Under Starmer, there was very little in terms of consultations, any discussions about anything at all.” Mainstream member Alex Sobel said: “I’ve had more meetings with No. 10 — I’ve been to No. 10 North — in these three months than the entire time of the previous administration.” One MP said: “People feel warmly towards Andy, which is half the battle. I think they trust his good intentions.” | Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images Bill Esterson, who chairs the Energy Security Committee, said he had “regular conversations with No. 10” and that Burnham’s team had “engaged very fully” with committee chairs and the PLP more broadly. A second 2024 intake MP said: “There’s definitely more of a concerted attempt for them to be reaching out and listening to us.” The days of being viewed “as the legal necessity to get legislation through” are over. 3) Burnham’s political instincts MPs reckon they’ve had an upgrade when it comes to raw political instincts. “There’s a feeling that we’ve got a guy up front who we can get behind,” said Opher. Advertisement Advertisement “He understands how politics works,” he added, citing the decision to delay approval for drilling at the Jackdaw gas field until after the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, where Labour faced a challenge from the Greens. “Andy’s much more savvy on what he’s doing.” Backbenchers also claim to feel more confident they won’t get caught in the Starmer flip-flop policy trap . The unnamed Socialist Campaign Group MP quoted above is still smarting over the “absolutely awful” two-child benefit cap vote, where rebels lost the whip only for it later to become government policy. The first 2024-intake MP reckons Burnham is better able to communicate difficult trade-offs, like altering the triple lock to fund social care. 4) Voters are giving Labour another chance It is ultimately Burnham’s popularity with the public that has fed into the positive mood. Many Labour MPs “agreed with the punters on the doorstep” about Starmer’s inadequacies, Opher said. Data showing Labour has retaken the opinion poll lead from Reform UK has boosted their optimism. “It doesn’t feel like a party that is about to be ripped apart,” he added. Advertisement The first 2024 intake MP said: “It has given us the right to be heard,” said the first 2024-intake Labour MP quoted above. “People feel warmly towards Andy, which is half the battle. I think they trust his good intentions.” MPs say Burnham’s administration is willing to recognize different views within the Labour Party. | Leon Neal/Getty Images Some flashpoints ahead… 1) The budget Burnham can only coast on the good vibes for so long, and the first test of tough political choices comes Wednesday in the budget. MPs on the left see the economic statement as a “crunch point” that will show if the chancellor will put his money where the PM’s mouth is. “If there’s an attempt to take money from ordinary people who’ve got nothing and no attempt to get finances from people who have got far too much, then probably there will be some sort of opposition”, said the unnamed Socialist Campaign Group MP previously quoted. They hope to see the already trailed bank tax confirmed, or a wealth tax. They warned that any decisions on what to cut and where to spend will pose “challenges from both sides of the PLP.” “The measure of Andy Burnham is how he deals with it,” they added. Advertisement 2) Welfare Burnham wants to avoid a repeat of the botched attempt at welfare reform which severely weakened Starmer’s authority. A long-awaited review by former Cabinet minister Alan Milburn into young people not in education, employment or training (NEETs) will be published shortly with recommendations. Milburn — alongside Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden — has been trying to ensure communication is better. “Pat has done an excellent job at building a consensus, rolling the carpet, setting out the argument, setting out the moral case, but he was doing that before the change of administration,” a third 2024-intake Labour MP said. The second 2024 Labour MP quoted above said most colleagues “feel like it’s a decent stab at it and it’s not come out of the blue.” Reasonable critics “were just getting stonewalled” last year. Esterson, who’s served in parliament since 2010, said regular engagement means “it’s not surprising that you get the benefit of the doubt far more often than if you don’t.” Advertisement 3) Europe Burnham’s admission that a future Labour manifesto could commit to a referendum on EU membership is already opening old Brexit wounds — and not in the way Labour wants. The Socialist Campaign Group MP previously quoted is uneasy about its potential to spark further division. “It nearly ripped the country apart and I’m not sure if it’s the right thing to do [to] reignite that horribleness in each constituency,” they said. The third 2024-intake Labour MP quoted above concurred. While people want a closer relationship with Europe, they believe rejoining is a “different kettle of fish” and jars with constituents who want “better public services and more economic growth” rather than continental renegotiations. 4) Energy Energy policy has already become a flashpoint. The decision to approve the Jackdaw gas field was met with some dissent. A decision about the larger Rosebank oil and gas field is still looming. Sobel told POLITICO’s London Playbook it “won’t make an impact on global prices and will give mixed messages in terms of investment in terms of both renewables and decarbonisation of home heating.” Left-wing Labour MPs also signed a letter to Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh urging her to reject the licenses due to climate change. “Every second we continue pumping fossil fuels into the atmosphere makes the crisis more severe,” the letter organized by Chris Hinchliff said . Advertisement The second 2024-intake MP quoted thought ministers are acting in good faith. “They’ve got one go at government and they seem to be doing their absolute best to give it a good whack,” they said. Sam Blewett contributed reporting .
